title: Telling stories & real conversation
goal: Tell a story with connectors, use relative clauses and reported speech, and sound natural with fillers, particles and a few idioms.
intro: Real Odia conversation is full of little words — **ମାନେ** 'I mean', **ତ** 'after all', **ନା** 'right?', **ହଉ**, **ଆରେ**, **ବାପରେ!** — and stories are tied together with **ପ୍ରଥମେ**, **ତା'ପରେ**, **ଶେଷରେ**. In this final unit you also learn how Odia builds 'the man *who* came' and 'she said *that*…', including the very Odia quotative **ବୋଲି**.

vocab.note: Marks the end of reported words or thoughts.

phrases.en: I mean… what I was saying was…
Listen, I'll tell you something funny.

grammar.title: Relative clauses: ଯେ- … ସେ- pairs and -ଥିବା
grammar.body:
Odia relative clauses come **before** the main clause and work in matched pairs — a **ଯ-word** in the relative clause, answered by a **ସ/ତ-word** in the main clause:
ଯିଏ … ସେ — who … he/she
ଯେଉଁ (noun) … ସେହି (noun) / ସେ — the … which … that
ଯେଉଁଠି … ସେଠି — where … there
ଯେତେବେଳେ … ସେତେବେଳେ — when … then
ଯାହା … ତାହା — what … that
ଯେତେ … ସେତେ — the more … the more

In everyday speech, a shorter alternative is a **participle** in front of the noun: **-ଥିବା** (who did/has done) or **-ଉଥିବା** (who is doing): କାଲି ଆସିଥିବା ଲୋକ 'the person who came yesterday', ଗୀତ ଗାଉଥିବା ଝିଅ 'the girl who is singing'.

examples.native: ଯିଏ ପରିଶ୍ରମ କରେ, ସେ ସଫଳ ହୁଏ।
examples.roman: jie pôrisrômô kôre, se sôphôḷô hue.

examples.native: ଯେଉଁ ଲୋକ କାଲି ଆସିଥିଲେ, ସେ ମୋ ମାମୁଁ।
examples.roman: jeuṃ lokô kali asithile, se mo mamuṃ.
examples.en: The man who came yesterday is my uncle.
The man who came yesterday is my uncle. (participle)

examples.native: ଯେତେବେଳେ ମୁଁ ପିଲା ଥିଲି, ସେତେବେଳେ ଗାଁରେ ରହୁଥିଲି।
examples.roman: jetebeḷe muṃ pila thili, setebeḷe gaṃre rôhuthili.
examples.en: When I was a child, I lived in a village.

examples.native: ମୁଁ ଯେଉଁଠି ରହେ, ସେଠି ବହୁତ ଗଛ ଅଛି।
examples.roman: muṃ jeuṃṭhi rôhe, seṭhi bôhutô gôchhô ôchhi.
examples.en: Where I live there are lots of trees.

grammar.title: Reported speech: ଯେ and ବୋଲି
grammar.body:
Two patterns:
1. **Verb + ଯେ + clause** (like English 'said that'): ସେ କହିଲା ଯେ ସେ କାଲି ଆସିବ.
2. **Clause + ବୋଲି + verb** — the more typically Odia way: ସେ କାଲି ଆସିବ ବୋଲି କହିଲା. ବୋଲି closes the quoted words, a bit like a spoken quotation mark.

The tense of the reported words usually stays as it was originally said (no 'backshift'): 'He said he *will* come'. Direct quotes are common too: ବୋଉ କହିଲେ, “ଶୀଘ୍ର ଆସ।”

**ବୋଲି** also gives a reason ('saying/thinking that…' → 'because'): ସେ ଅସୁସ୍ଥ ବୋଲି ଆସିଲା ନାହିଁ 'he didn't come because he's ill'.

examples.native: ସେ କହିଲା ଯେ ସେ କାଲି ଆସିବ।
examples.roman: se kôhila je se kali asibô.
examples.en: He/She said that he/she'd come tomorrow.
He/She didn't come because he/she is ill.

grammar.title: Sounding natural: particles, fillers and idioms
grammar.body:
**Particles** placed after a word change its tone: **ତ** adds 'after all / you know' (ମୁଁ ତ ଜାଣେ 'well, *I* know'); **ହିଁ** means 'only / exactly' (ଏବେ ହିଁ 'right now'); **ବି** 'also'; **ନା** at the end asks for agreement ('…, right?'); **କି** at the end makes a yes/no question.

**Fillers**: ମାନେ 'I mean', ହଉ 'okay', ଆଚ୍ଛା 'right…', ଦେଖ 'look…', କଥା କ'ଣ କି 'the thing is…'. **Exclamations**: ଆରେ! 'hey!', ବାପରେ! 'wow / oh no!', ହାୟ ହାୟ 'oh dear'.

A few common sayings: ଆପଣା ହାତ ଜଗନ୍ନାଥ 'one's own hand is Jagannath' (if you want something done, do it yourself); ମୁଣ୍ଡରେ ହାତ ଦେଇ ବସିବା 'to sit with one's hand on one's head' (to be at one's wits' end); ନାଚି ନ ଜାଣି ଅଗଣା ଦୋଷ 'can't dance, blames the courtyard' (a bad workman blames his tools).

examples.en: Well, I don't know (don't ask me).
Come on, let's go right now.
If you want it done, do it yourself. (lit. one's own hand is Jagannath)

examples.native: ଖବର ଶୁଣି ସେ ମୁଣ୍ଡରେ ହାତ ଦେଇ ବସିଗଲେ।
examples.roman: khôbôrô suṇi se muṇḍôre hatô dei bôsigôle.
examples.en: Hearing the news, he/she sat down in despair.
A bad workman blames his tools. (lit. can't dance — 'it's the courtyard's fault!')

dialogue.title: Bapi's story
dialogue.setting: Over tea, Bapi tells Sam about a visit to his uncle's village.

lines.speaker: Bapi
lines.en: Listen, I'll tell you something funny.

lines.speaker: Bapi
lines.native: ଗତ ସପ୍ତାହରେ ମୁଁ ମୋ ମାମୁଙ୍କ ଗାଁକୁ ଯାଇଥିଲି। ପ୍ରଥମେ ବସରେ ଗଲି, ତା'ପରେ ଅଟୋରେ।
lines.roman: gôtô sôptahôre muṃ mo mamuṅkô gaṃku jaithili. prôthôme bôsôre gôli, tapôre ôṭore.
lines.en: Last week I went to my uncle's village. First I went by bus, then by auto.

lines.speaker: Bapi
lines.native: ଯେଉଁଠି ଅଟୋ ଅଟକିଲା, ସେଠି ଜଣେ ବୁଢ଼ା ଲୋକ ଠିଆ ହୋଇଥିଲେ।
lines.roman: jeuṃṭhi ôṭo ôṭôkila, seṭhi jôṇe buṛha lokô ṭhia hoithile.
lines.en: Where the auto stopped, an old man was standing.

lines.speaker: Bapi
lines.native: ମୁଁ ମାମୁଙ୍କ ଘର ବିଷୟରେ ପଚାରିଲି। ସେ ସିଧା ଯାଇ ବାଁକୁ ବୁଲିବାକୁ କହିଲେ।
lines.roman: muṃ mamuṅkô ghôrô bisôyôre pôcharili. se sidha jai baṃku bulibaku kôhile.
lines.en: I asked him about my uncle's house. He told me to go straight and turn left.

lines.speaker: Bapi
lines.native: ମୁଁ ଘଣ୍ଟେ ଚାଲିଲି, କିନ୍ତୁ ଘର ମିଳିଲା ନାହିଁ! ଭାରି ଭୋକ ଲାଗୁଥିଲା।
lines.roman: muṃ ghôṇṭe chalili, kintu ghôrô miḷila nahiṃ! bhari bhokô laguthila.
lines.en: I walked for an hour but couldn't find the house! I was starving.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.en: Oh no! What happened in the end?

lines.speaker: Bapi
lines.native: ଶେଷରେ ଜାଣିଲି ଯେ ସେଇ ବୁଢ଼ା ଲୋକ ହିଁ ମୋ ମାମୁଁ! ଦଶ ବର୍ଷ ପରେ ଦେଖୁଥିଲି ବୋଲି ଚିହ୍ନିପାରିଲି ନାହିଁ।
lines.roman: sesôre jaṇili je sei buṛha lokô hiṃ mo mamuṃ! dôsô bôrsô pôre dekhuthili boli chinhiparili nahiṃ.
lines.en: In the end I found out that the old man WAS my uncle! I hadn't seen him for ten years, so I didn't recognise him.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.native: ହା ହା! ଆଉ ସେ ତୁମକୁ ଚିହ୍ନିଲେ ନାହିଁ?
lines.roman: ha ha! au se tumôku chinhile nahiṃ?
lines.en: Ha ha! And he didn't recognise you?

lines.speaker: Bapi
lines.native: ସେ କହିଲେ, “ମୁଁ ଭାବିଲି ତୁମେ ଜଣେ ଟୁରିଷ୍ଟ!”
lines.roman: se kôhile, “muṃ bhabili tume jôṇe ṭurisṭ!”
lines.en: He said, 'I thought you were a tourist!'

culture: Odisha has a rich storytelling tradition: grandmothers' tales (ଜେଜେମା ଗପ), the medieval *Odia Bhagabata* of Jagannath Das recited in village halls (*bhagabata tungi*), and modern literature from Fakir Mohan Senapati — the father of Odia fiction — to Jnanpith winners such as Gopinath Mohanty and Sitakant Mahapatra. Chatting (ଗପ କରିବା) over tea at the *chhak* or on the veranda in the evening is a favourite pastime: the best way to practise everything you've learned. ଶୁଭେଚ୍ଛା — good luck!
